Dear unmarkers,

I am trying to simulate data under an N-mixture model with a negative binomial mixture for latent abundance N using R function rnbinom(n, size, prob, mu). Part of what the R help file says is this:

"An alternative parametrization (often used in ecology) is by the mean  mu, and size, the dispersion parameter, where  prob = size/(size+mu)."

So, I simulate the latent N's as this, where beta0=1, beta1=-1 and dispersion = 10 in my first trial:

x1 <- seq(-2, 2,, M)       # Site covariate

lambda <- exp(beta0 + beta1 * x1)

size <- dispersion      # Dispersion parameter

N <- rnbinom(n = length(x), mu = lambda, size = dispersion)

(I also have a detection model with one observational covariate, but that's of no importance here.)

When I simulate 100 data sets and analyse them in unmarked using pcount with the data-generating model, I get what look like unbiased estimates for the regression parameters (red is the truth, blue the mean of 100 estimates), but the estimates of the "dispersion parameter" are way off; see attached figure.

Does anybody know how the dispersion parameter in unmarked is defined ?

Thanks and kind regards  --  Marc

# Simulate Nmix data with NegBin abundance distribution

NB.data <- function(M = 267, T = 3, alpha0 = 1, alpha1 = -1, beta0 = -1, beta1 = 1, dispersion = 10){

# Function simulates data for the Nmix model with
# a negative binomial abundance distribution.

# alpha0 and alpha1 are the intercept and the slope of a logistic-linear
# regression of detection probability on an observation covariate x2.

# beta0 and beta1 are the intercept and the slope of a log-linear
# regression of expected abundance on a site covariate x1.

# M is the number of sites and T the number of temporal reps.

# dispersion is the negative binomial dispersion parameter, with
# lower values corresponding to increasing aggregation.

# Abundance model

x1 <- seq(-2, 2,, M)       # Site covariate

lambda <- exp(beta0 + beta1 * x1)

size <- dispersion      # Dispersion parameter

N <- rnbinom(n = length(x), mu = lambda, size = dispersion)

par(mfrow = c(2,2))

plot(x1, lambda, main = "Relationship x1-lambda")

hist(N, main = "Histogram of latent N", breaks = 50, col = "grey")

# Detection model

x2 <- matrix(rnorm(M*T), ncol = T)    # Observational covariate

p <- plogis(alpha0 + alpha1 * x2)

plot(x2, p, main = "Relationship x2-p")

C <- array(dim = c(M,T))

for(j in 1:T){

   C[,j] <- rbinom(M, N, p[,j])

}

hist(C, main = "Histogram of counts C", breaks = 50, col = "grey")

# Output

return(list(M=M, T=T, alpha0=alpha0, alpha1=alpha1, beta0=beta0, beta1=beta1, dispersion=dispersion, x1=x1, x2=x2, lambda=lambda, N=N, p=p, C=C))

}

# Check how it works

NB.data()

NB.data(alpha1=0, beta1=0)

NB.data(alpha1=-2, beta1=2)

NB.data(alpha1=-2, beta1=2, dispersion = 0.1)

NB.data(alpha0=0, alpha1=1, beta0 = 1, beta1=-1, dispersion = 10)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I apologize if this question ends up being more about R than unmarked.  I'm still learning my way around unmarked and R.

GOAL:
I am trying to write a program to do backwards selection for covariates to enter a pcount model. I want to specify a starting model, e.g.:

m00 <- pcount(~ a + b + c + d, ~1, umf, K=300, mixture="P", engine="C")

...then look at the unmarkedFitPCount object and review the P(>|z|) for covariates a, b, c, and d.  If the p-val of one or more covariates > alpha, choose the covariate with the largest p-val and remove it.  Run another model (m01) without that covariate.  Repeat until no covariates are included, or all are significant. messages.body_plain:
I don't have a complete answer (yet) but I two observations:

(1) I agree that extreme values of psi1 are worth looking into (when you run it forward), but such an extreme value is also what you would get if psi1 is close to 1.0.  Is psi1 approximately equal to 1.0 a possibility with your data?

(2) The pdf that I attached earlier assumed that each transition period would have a separate epsilon and gamma.  But your model makes the restriction that all the epsilon's are equal across time and all of the gamma's are equal across seasons.  While one can construct the reverse Markov chain model that gives equivalent history probabilities (which also give equivalent psi's), the epsilon's and gamma's needed to do that must vary over seasons.  (I can at least prove that for 3 seasons and then would assume that holds for more than 3 seasons.)  So fitting in the reverse direction with that same restriction won't result in the same Markov chain model.

Jim

messages.subject_clean: condition number for matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

we are fitting dynamic occupancy models to a relatively sparse data set (80 sites, about 15 years, 3 reps per year). With easily 10 covariates to choose from (not including YEAR), the model complexity/information content ratio becomes an issue. For instance, we have lots of boundary estimates and very large SE's, indicating numerical problems.

As a further indication of numerical problems, I thought we could use the condition number, which is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of either the Hessian matrix or the variance-covariance matrix (and whether it's the former or the latter is exactly my first question):

max(eigen(hessian(fitted.model.object))$values)/min(eigen(hessian(fitted.model.object))$values)

According to a Wikipedia entry, values greater than 30 indicate problems. However, we get values that are several orders of magnitude greater than that even for models for which the MLE point estimates and SE's seem to look fine.

Does anybody have experience in that and could give some advice ?

Thanks and kind regards  --- Marc

Marc, Richard,
Thanks for the suggestions - you both had good points.  I ended up using pcount with pdredge in MuMIn and working out a model selection approach first using backwards stepwise selection to work down from a set of 11 detection covariates to 8, then comparing all subsets of the remaining 8 to arrive at a set of detection covariates.  Then I kept those detection covariates in a model with my full set of potential abundance covariates and ran that through all subsets using pdredge again.  At each stage, I selected the best model according to AICc.

This seemed to produce fairly reasonable models for some of my species in terms of abundance estimates, though they all seem a bit high.  For my Indigo Bunting models, however, I am getting absurdly large abundance (25 birds / 50 m count circle) and low prob of detection (0.06) estimates, despite this species being the one for which I had the most detections.  I have tried being more selective with my potential covariates, limiting them to 3 or 4 for abundance and detection, but pdredge selects out everything, leaving me with a null model.  I also tried model averaging to combine all models with delta AIC < 2, (even tried delta AIC < 4) and my estimates are nearly the same.

I'm sort of banging my head against the wall here.  Any suggestions on where to go with this next?

Dear all,

I run a "simple" hierarchical distance sampling analysis for data collected along 24 transects of very variable length (mean = 1000 m, range = 270-2510). I have a question about how to incorporate transect length into the analysis. I am a little confused, since I can put length as a covariate into the unmarked data frame, but then there is also the tlength argument in the unmarkedFrameDS function. Is the following reasoning sensible ?

I put length (unscaled) into the data frame as a site-level covariate and then use 'offset(length)' in the linear predictor for abundance. That way, I model density. However, I also clearly need the vector of lengths in the 'tlength' argument, because that information is needed when the distsamp function returns the estimates at the abundance rather than the density scale.

Thanks for comments, and sorry if this is an obvious question....

Regards  --  Marc
